sections.h2: Who values my house for Ohio property tax?
sections.html:
The county auditor values every parcel in the county, and the tax bill follows from that value. Ohio's Department of Taxation describes a full reappraisal every six years, with a triennial update between reappraisals that adjusts values from recent sales and market trends without a physical visit.

Once the value is set, a millage rate turns it into a bill. Ohio's tax resource hub explains that inside mills are set by local governments without a vote, while outside mills come from voter-approved levies for schools, fire service and similar needs. That is why a bill can rise even when a house keeps the same value: a new levy changes the rate. The rate itself cannot be argued in a valuation complaint, only the value can.

An owner who thinks the auditor's number is too high has two routes, described on the Department of Taxation property tax page. Some counties offer an informal review, usually in reappraisal years, and every county has the formal complaint to its Board of Revision. Ask the auditor's office which one applies to your parcel.

sections.h2: When is Ohio property tax due, and what happens if I am late?
sections.html:
Under R.C. 323.12, the full year is payable by December 31, or half of the current taxes plus any delinquent taxes by that date and the other half by June 20 of the next year. In many counties the actual due dates land later, because R.C. 323.17 lets payment move to January 31 and July 20 when delivery of the tax duplicate is delayed. Your bill shows the dates that apply to your parcel.

A payment counts as on time if the treasurer receives it by the last day, or if it arrives in an envelope postmarked by the U.S. Postal Service on or before that day. A private meter postmark does not count. The treasurer may also keep the books open a little longer to process payments.

Late payment carries a price under R.C. 323.121:

  • A ten percent penalty goes on the unpaid half if it is missed by the December 31 date, or the extended date.
  • A like ten percent penalty goes on the balance of the unpaid current taxes if the total is not paid by June 20, or the extended date.
  • Interest then runs on delinquent taxes at the rate set under section 5703.47.

sections.h2: How do I file a Board of Revision complaint in Ohio?
sections.html:
File a complaint with the county auditor on or before March 31 of the following tax year, or the date the first-half collection closes, whichever is later. That is the rule in R.C. 5715.19. The auditor hands every complaint to the county Board of Revision, and the postmark on a mailed complaint counts as the filing date.

The statute lets an owner, the owner's spouse, a tenant of commercial or industrial property in some leases, and certain retained professionals file. A designated appraiser, a licensed real estate broker and a public accountant are on that list when retained by the owner. Ohio's tax department suggests gathering recent sales of comparable homes, an independent appraisal if you have one, and photos that show the house's condition.

One limit surprises people. If you filed a complaint on a parcel in an earlier year of the same interim period, you cannot file again unless something changed after the tax lien date. The statute names four changes:

  • The property sold in an arm's length transaction.
  • The property lost value because of a casualty.
  • A substantial improvement was added.
  • Occupancy rose or fell by at least fifteen percent with a substantial economic effect.

If the Board of Revision rules against you, R.C. 5717.01 allows an appeal to the Board of Tax Appeals within thirty days after the board of revision mails notice of its decision.

sections.h2: What is the Ohio homestead exemption and who can claim it?
sections.html:
The homestead exemption trims the tax on an owner-occupied home for qualifying people. R.C. 323.152 covers persons who are permanently and totally disabled, persons sixty-five or older, certain surviving spouses, disabled veterans and the surviving spouses of public service officers killed in the line of duty. R.C. 323.151 defines the terms: a home includes up to one acre of surrounding land, and "sixty-five or older" means the person turned sixty-four before January 1 of the application year.

For most applicants the reduction is tied to a slice of the home's true value, with the statute naming twenty-five thousand dollars for the base reduction, adjusted each year for inflation by the tax commissioner. Disabled veterans and the surviving spouses of public service officers killed in the line of duty get a larger slice of fifty thousand dollars, with no income test. Everyone else faces an income ceiling, written in the statute as thirty thousand dollars of total income and adjusted yearly. The auditor can tell you the current figure.

The same section also sets a partial exemption on any homestead, a percentage of the tax from qualifying levies. The text lists 5.70 percent for the first tax year the amendment applies, then 8.92 percent, 12.15 percent, and 15.38 percent for the third following year and every year after. Ask the county auditor which step your tax year falls on.

Applications go to the county auditor on forms from the Department of Taxation: DTE 105A for most applicants, DTE 105I for disabled veterans and their surviving spouses, and DTE 105K for surviving spouses of public service officers. Once approved, an owner does not need to reapply each year unless eligibility changes. The separate owner-occupancy credit applies to a primary residence the owner lived in on January 1 of the year of application.

sections.h2: What happens to the property tax when I sell an Ohio house?
sections.html:
The lien for each year's tax attaches to the real property on January 1 and continues until the tax, penalties and interest are paid, according to R.C. 323.11. A sale does not erase it. The unpaid amount has to be cleared from the sale money or the buyer takes the property with it. Ask the county treasurer for a payoff figure before the closing date.

At the deed stage, R.C. 319.202 asks the grantee to submit a statement of value to the auditor. That statement must confirm the grantor was asked whether the property's taxes are reduced by the homestead exemption, and it must address current agricultural use valuation. A buyer who does not qualify for a reduction the seller received should expect the bill to change.

Owners already behind on tax have a way out of foreclosure. R.C. 323.31 gives an owner who lives in the home at least one chance to enter a written delinquent tax contract with the county treasurer. For owner-occupied residential property the period cannot exceed five years, and it runs at least two years if the owner asks. A missed installment or unpaid current taxes voids the contract, and it is not available while a tax certificate or foreclosure judgment is outstanding.

faqs.q: When is the Ohio Board of Revision complaint deadline?
faqs.a: The deadline is March 31 of the following tax year, or the close of first-half collection if that is later. File with the county auditor, who passes it to the Board of Revision. A mailed complaint is treated as filed on the postmark date.

faqs.q: Does Ohio let me pay property tax in installments?
faqs.a: Yes, in two halves. The statute sets the halves at December 31 and June 20, and the dates move to January 31 and July 20 when delivery of the duplicate is delayed. Your bill shows which dates apply.

faqs.q: Can I get a homestead exemption if I am under sixty-five?
faqs.a: Yes, if you are permanently and totally disabled on January 1 of the application year, or if you are a disabled veteran or a qualifying surviving spouse. The statute also provides a partial exemption on any homestead. Apply through the county auditor.

faqs.q: Who sets the Ohio millage rate?
faqs.a: Local governments set inside mills, and voters approve outside mills through levies. The rate cannot be changed by a valuation complaint. Only the property's value can be challenged at the Board of Revision.

faqs.q: What if I cannot pay my Ohio property tax on a home I live in?
faqs.a: Ask the county treasurer about a delinquent tax contract. An owner who lives in the home is entitled to one, payable over up to five years. Entering it before a foreclosure judgment keeps the county from filing suit while installments are paid.
